name: Castilleja

priority: colored bracts and calyx tips versus the true corolla
predominant bract/calyx color in the two perennial species
upper-leaf and bract lobing as supporting characters
study_strategy.warning: Do not key these by bract color or leaf lobing alone. Castilleja indivisa is the strongest first split because it is annual; C. purpurea and C. lindheimeri are perennial members of the C. purpurea complex and may intergrade where they meet. Current Kew/POWO treats C. lindheimeri as an accepted species rather than merely C. purpurea var. lindheimeri.

quick_split: C. indivisa — annual Texas paintbrush, usually compact with vivid scarlet-orange bracts.
C. purpurea — perennial prairie paintbrush with variable bract color; rocky calcareous prairie.
C. lindheimeri — perennial Edwards Plateau endemic; upper leaves commonly 2–3-lobed, orange-red bracts, glandular inflorescence.

shared_genus_pattern.what_they_share: Green photosynthetic root hemiparasites with alternate leaves, a terminal bracted flowering spike, strongly bilateral tubular flowers, and a dry many-seeded capsule. Much of the bright paintbrush display is produced by colored floral bracts and calyx tissue rather than broad petals.
shared_genus_pattern.look_here_first: Photograph the WHOLE plant first so annual versus perennial habit is not lost. Then take a side-on close-up of one flowering spike. In that close-up identify the colored BRACT below each flower, the colored CALYX around the flower base, and the narrower projecting COROLLA. Only after those parts are separated should color, lobing, hairs, and proportions be used for species comparison.
shared_genus_pattern.memory_rule: INDIVISA = annual Texas paintbrush. PURPUREA and LINDHEIMERI = perennial prairie-paintbrush complex; purple/pink-purple is typical purpurea and red/orange is typical lindheimeri, but intermediates and hybrids mean color is a guide rather than a guarantee.

comparison_matrix.Castilleja indivisa: Annual. Usually a compact spring paintbrush without the persistent perennial base of the prairie-paintbrush complex.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja purpurea: Perennial, often several-stemmed from the base.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja lindheimeri: Perennial, often several-stemmed from the base.

comparison_matrix.Castilleja indivisa: Usually vivid scarlet to orange-red; color alone is not diagnostic.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja purpurea: Typical plants are purple to pink-purple, but red, orange, peach, yellow, cream, and rarely white expressions occur.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja lindheimeri: Typical plants are red, reddish-orange, or orange.

comparison_matrix.Castilleja indivisa: Upper foliage and bracts form the compact colored spike; use shape only with the annual habit and flower details.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja purpurea: Upper leaves may become lobed; lobing is supporting rather than decisive.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja lindheimeri: Upper leaves commonly divide into 2–3 narrow lobes and bracts are commonly 3-lobed; proximal leaves may remain entire.

comparison_matrix.Castilleja indivisa: Common spring paintbrush of Texas prairies, roadsides, and open ground.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja purpurea: Rocky/calcareous prairie, limestone roadbanks, hills, ledges, and related open habitats.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja lindheimeri: Edwards Plateau and nearby rocky limestone grassland, roadbank, slope, ridge, and open juniper/oak settings.

comparison_matrix.Castilleja indivisa: Can hybridize with members of the C. purpurea complex, including documented C. indivisa × C. lindheimeri material in Hays County.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja purpurea: May intergrade/hybridize with C. lindheimeri near contact zones and with C. indivisa in some areas.
comparison_matrix.Castilleja lindheimeri: May intergrade/hybridize with C. purpurea near contact zones and with C. indivisa in Hays County.

field_key: 1. Plant annual → start with Castilleja indivisa. Confirm with the compact Texas-paintbrush habit and spike structure; do not rely on red color by itself.
2. Plant perennial → C. purpurea complex. Photograph the whole plant base plus a side-on flowering spike.
3. Perennial with predominantly purple or pink-purple bract/calyx apices → typical C. purpurea, after checking the rest of the character set.
4. Perennial with predominantly red to reddish-orange/orange bract/calyx apices → typical C. lindheimeri, after checking upper-leaf/bract lobing and regional context.
5. Mixed, intermediate, or contradictory characters → leave as Castilleja purpurea-complex / possible intergrade until a specimen-level review. Do not force a color-only species call.
overlap_and_cautions: The showy colored structures are mostly floral bracts and calyx tissue; the true corolla is the narrower tubular flower projecting from them.
Bract color is useful in the C. purpurea complex but not absolute. C. purpurea can occur in colors other than purple, and hybrid/intergrade plants exist.
Leaf lobing is supporting evidence only. C. lindheimeri can have entire lower/proximal leaves, and lobing varies with position on the stem.
Do not uproot a paintbrush to prove hemiparasitism. Root haustoria are a biological family trait, not a field character worth damaging the plant to see.
A single nearby grass or forb in a photograph does not prove that exact individual is the host plant.
Older records labeled C. purpurea var. lindheimeri belong to the current C. lindheimeri learner concept only after explicit synonym reconciliation.

visual_comparison.subtitle: Seven physical project images currently exist: three C. indivisa, three C. purpurea, and one private-study C. lindheimeri habitat frame. The first two species have useful bract/flower views; C. lindheimeri still lacks a rights-cleared diagnostic close-up.

visual_comparison.unresolved_photo_gap: Castilleja lindheimeri still needs a physically installed, rights-safe side-on flowering-spike close-up that clearly shows colored bract, calyx, projecting corolla, upper-leaf/bract lobing, and visible pubescence if present. Do not substitute an unverified web photo just to fill the slot.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.purpose: Rights-safe side view showing one colored bract, calyx, projecting corolla, upper leaf/bract lobing, and hairs where visible. This is the largest current visual gap.
Same-angle, similar-scale side views for indivisa, purpurea, and lindheimeri so color is taught together with actual structure rather than as a standalone cue.
Teach annual indivisa versus perennial purpurea/lindheimeri without uprooting plants.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.role: leaf series from lower to upper stem
diagnostic_photo_checklist.purpose: Show that lobing changes with stem position and prevent the false rule that every C. lindheimeri leaf must be lobed.
Arrow the bract, calyx, corolla tube/beak, and stigma so learners stop calling every colored part a petal.
Connect Castilleja back to the Orobanchaceae many-seeded capsule family character.
When a rights-safe, confidently identified specimen is available, show why intermediate color/lobing should be left unresolved rather than forced.
